$comment: The reference performance environment (R1).
R1 has been open since MVP-0 for one reason: numbers measured on a developer workstation are
indicative only, and nothing stopped one being labelled as though it were calibrated. The
environment id was a free-text variable copied straight into the baseline, so
RAMALS_PERF_ENV=perf-standard-01 on a laptop produced a file claiming to be authoritative. The
label was a claim about the run rather than evidence of it.
This file is the other half of that claim. attest.py measures the host and the running
containers against it, and run-baseline.sh refuses to stamp a qualified id on a run that did
not match. Owning the right hardware does not close R1 on its own -- without the check, a
laptop can still assert the label.
COMPARABILITY BY CONSTRAINT, NOT BY IDENTICAL HARDWARE.
Requiring one exact machine makes the baseline unreproducible the moment that machine is
replaced. Instead the system under test runs under pinned CPU and memory limits, and the host
is required to have enough headroom that those limits -- rather than contention -- decide what
the run measures. Two hosts that both satisfy this produce comparable numbers even when their
totals differ. What cannot be constrained away is recorded instead: CPU model and kernel go
into the attestation so a later reader can see whether two baselines share a processor class.
WHERE THESE NUMBERS COME FROM.
They are a reasoned starting point, not a measurement. The MVP-0 indicative run met every
request-class budget at 60 rps on a 12-CPU / 7.6 GiB workstation with the load generator, the
backend and the database all sharing one host. The limits below give the system under test
more headroom than that arrangement had, and move the generator off the host so it stops
competing with what it is measuring.
status is 'proposed' deliberately: the first calibrated run on a registered host confirms or
revises these values, and only then does the spec become 'reference'. A spec that declared
itself authoritative before anything had been measured against it would be the same kind of
unearned claim this file exists to prevent.
Headroom, so the pinned limits below are what bounds the run. min_cpus is the sum of the
container limits plus room for the kernel, the container runtime and the database's own I/O
threads. A host that only just fits the limits measures scheduling contention.
Every service under test must carry an explicit limit. An unpinned container inherits the
whole host, which is precisely what makes two runs on different machines incomparable.
performance/compose.perf-fixed.yml sets these; the attestation checks what is actually
running rather than what a file says.
The load generator must not run on the host it is measuring. On the MVP-0 workstation run it
did, so k6's own CPU time was taken from the system under test and the reported latency
included that interference. This is the requirement that cannot be met by resource limits
alone, and the one that needs a second machine.
Facts that cannot be required without pinning the baseline to one machine, but that change
the numbers enough that a reader must be able to see them. Recorded in every attestation.
